items.title: Energy can be lost in a collision; momentum cannot
items.claim: Two cars crash and lock together. Their combined kinetic energy after the collision is LESS than before (energy lost to heat, sound, deformation). But the combined momentum is exactly the same.
items.prompt: Why does momentum survive while energy doesn't?

options.text: Momentum is always conserved; energy is not

Total energy is conserved if you include heat, sound, deformation — but KINETIC energy alone is not conserved in inelastic collisions. Momentum is a vector quantity conserved by Newton's third law independent of internal energy losses
Momentum and energy are equally lost
Energy conservation only applies to electricity

items.reveal_title: Conservation laws and what they refer to
items.reveal:
Newton's third law (action and reaction) implies that internal forces in a closed system cancel pairwise. Total momentum (m1 v1 + m2 v2 + ...) does not change unless an external force acts.

This holds regardless of whether the collision is elastic (kinetic energy conserved) or inelastic (kinetic energy partly converted to heat, deformation, etc.).

Kinetic energy = (1/2) m v^2 — proportional to v squared, so velocity SIGN doesn't matter (kinetic energy is scalar and always positive). Two equal-mass objects approaching each other with v and -v have total KE > 0 but total momentum = 0. After perfectly inelastic collision (stuck together), final velocity = 0, KE = 0. KE is lost; momentum unchanged.

Elastic collisions (snooker balls, gas molecules): both momentum and kinetic energy conserved.
Inelastic collisions (cars sticking, putty hitting wall): momentum conserved; some KE -> heat/sound/deformation.
Explosions (reverse collisions): momentum still conserved (must be balanced); KE can INCREASE (from chemical energy released).

The full energy conservation includes all forms: chemical, thermal, acoustic, electromagnetic. It's the kinetic energy alone that can vary.

The distinction is crucial for understanding everything from billiard balls to particle accelerators to car crashes to firearms.
items.why: Conservation laws are taught as universal. Different conservation laws apply to different quantities and conditions. Energy is always conserved (with all forms counted); kinetic energy alone is not.

items.title: Half the world's billionaires got there partly by luck
items.claim: Repeated coin flips produce some very lucky streaks. The proportion of 'successful' (still in business, in market, alive) entities at the top of a population sample is dominated by selection effects — the unsuccessful disappear from view, leaving the survivors looking exceptional.

options.text: Survivorship bias: we only see the successes, and infer skill from outcomes; randomness alone would have produced some 'winners' from a starting pool, but we don't see the matching losers

items.reveal_title: Survivorship bias and the law of large pools
items.reveal:
If 10,000 hedge fund managers each pick stocks randomly for 10 years, about (1/1024) * 10,000 ≈ 10 will have called the market right 10 years running (by pure luck). These 10 will be on the cover of business magazines, will publish books on their 'secrets', and will attract investor billions.

The other 9,990 are out of business and forgotten.

Mochon and Norton (2011, 2012) replicated this in the lab: random stock-picking among 'subjects' produced 'expert' track records statistically indistinguishable from actual hedge funds. Selection of survivors creates the illusion of skill.

Real-world cases:
- WWII US bombers: aircraft returning from missions had bullet holes in wings and fuselage, not engines or cockpits. The Air Force initially considered reinforcing where the holes were — until Abraham Wald pointed out: planes hit in the engine or cockpit don't return. Reinforce the unhit areas.
- Famous 'success stories' (Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, J.K. Rowling) tell entrepreneurs what to do — but tens of thousands who tried the same things failed.
- Stock market: survivor-bias-corrected returns are ~1-2% per year lower than uncorrected indices, because failed stocks drop out.

The correct statistical question is not 'what did successful X do?' but 'what's the base rate of success among everyone who tried that?'.
items.why: Success seems instructive. Survivorship bias means we systematically learn from outliers and ignore the (invisible) ordinary cases. The math of selection effects is more important than the stories of any individual.

items.title: Centrifugal force doesn't exist — except when it does
items.claim: Physics teachers often say 'centrifugal force isn't real'. In an inertial reference frame, that's correct — only centripetal force exists. But in a ROTATING frame (sitting in a car going round a corner), centrifugal force is a genuine, calculable, predictive force.
items.prompt: What's the relationship between the two?

options.text: They are the same force renamed

Centripetal force is the inward force that keeps an object circling (real in any frame); centrifugal force is the apparent OUTWARD force in a rotating frame — fictitious in inertial frames but necessary for Newton's laws to hold in rotating ones
Only one of them is real, but textbooks disagree which

items.reveal:
Newton's laws hold in inertial (non-accelerating) frames. To make them hold in a rotating (accelerating) frame, you must add fictitious forces — apparent forces that arise from the frame's acceleration, not from any physical interaction.

In a rotating frame at angular velocity omega, two fictitious forces:
- Centrifugal: F = m * omega^2 * r, outward.
- Coriolis: F = -2 m omega cross v, perpendicular to motion.

For a passenger in a car going around a curve at constant speed:
- Inertial (road) frame: the only real force is the inward (centripetal) friction from the seat. The car turns; the passenger tends to continue straight, hence pushes against the door.
- Rotating (car) frame: the passenger feels pushed outward — centrifugal force. The frame is accelerating; the passenger needs to invoke centrifugal force to make Newton's laws work.

Both descriptions give the same observable outcome. The 'centrifugal' force is real in the car's frame in the sense that you must include it to do correct mechanics; it's 'fictitious' in the road's frame in the sense that no physical object is pushing.

Earth's rotation: Coriolis force (small at human scales) deflects winds and ocean currents — counterclockwise around northern lows, clockwise around southern lows. The Earth's frame is rotating; the Coriolis force must be included.

In general relativity, all forces of inertia (centrifugal, Coriolis, gravity) become 'fictitious' in the right sense — geometry of spacetime, not push-pull.
items.why: The 'centrifugal is fictitious' rule is true in one frame but missing the point. Both forces are correct in their proper frames. The debate is about reference-frame choice, not physics.
